Surgical Breast Enlargement

Breast Augmentation: Implants & Fat Transfer

Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure designed to increase breast volume or alter breast shape using implants or, in selected cases, the patient’s own fat.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast Augmentation: Implants & Fat Transfer

It may be considered by people seeking greater fullness, a change in proportions, or restoration of volume following pregnancy or weight change. Treatment planning should account for anatomy, existing breast tissue, skin characteristics, general health, lifestyle, expectations and the individual’s willingness to accept surgical risks and future follow-up.

Breast augmentation: data from the American Society of Plastic Surgeons

The figures and lists below summarise patient information published by the American Society of Plastic Surgeons (ASPS), the largest association of board-certified plastic surgeons in the United States. They are reproduced here for education and context. ASPS guidance reflects United States practice and regulation and does not replace assessment by a suitably qualified clinician in your own jurisdiction.

ASPS patient information

What breast augmentation can — and cannot — do

What breast augmentation can — and cannot — do
GoalWhat ASPS patient information says
Increase fullness and projectionBreast implants or fat transfer can increase the size and projection of the breasts.
Improve balance and proportionAugmentation can improve the balance between breast and hip contours.
Support body imageASPS notes the procedure may enhance self-image and self-confidence.
Breast reconstructionImplants may also be used for breast reconstruction after mastectomy or injury.
Severe droopingAugmentation alone does not correct severely drooping breasts; a breast lift may be needed, at the same time or as a separate operation.

ASPS patient information

How the procedure is usually performed

ASPS describes the operation in five broad stages.

01

Anesthesia

Intravenous sedation or general anaesthesia is used, so the procedure is comfortable throughout.

02

Incision

Peri-areolar, inframammary fold or axillary incisions are the usual routes; ASPS notes that the belly-button approach carries a higher complication rate.

03

Placement

The implant is placed either under the pectoral muscle (submuscular) or behind the breast tissue over the muscle (subglandular).

04

Closure

Layered sutures close the tissue, with sutures, skin adhesive or surgical tape on the skin. Scars fade over time and are affected by genetics, nicotine and infection.

05

Results

Results are visible immediately, with the final shape settling as swelling resolves.

ASPS patient information

Types of breast implants

Types of breast implants
ImplantWhat ASPS patient information says
SalineSterile salt water; collapses and is absorbed or expelled if the shell leaks; uniform shape and firmness; FDA-approved from age 18.
Structured salineSalt water with an internal structure for a more natural feel.
Silicone gelGel feels more like natural breast tissue; does not collapse if it leaks; regular ultrasound or MRI screening is advised; FDA-approved from age 22.
Form-stable (“gummy bear”)Keeps its shape even if the shell breaks; firmer and thicker; a shaped version gives more bottom projection but can look unusual if it rotates; requires a longer incision.
RoundGenerally a fuller look; higher profiles add more projection; less concern about rotation.
SmoothSoftest feel and natural movement, but rippling may be felt or seen.
TexturedTissue adheres to the surface so it is less likely to move and may reduce capsular contracture, but textured surfaces are where BIA-ALCL occurs most often.

Recovery and results (ASPS patient information)

  • Immediately after surgery the breasts are wrapped in gauze, with an elastic bandage or support bra to limit swelling and support healing.
  • Patients are monitored in recovery and are usually permitted home about an hour after surgery once stable for discharge.
  • The support garment (a bra or elastic band) is worn around the clock as instructed; wound care instructions differ between surgeons and should be followed exactly.
  • Acute pain typically subsides after one to five days, but soreness and swelling may persist for a few weeks.
  • Final results settle over a few weeks as swelling subsides; incision lines may take several months to a couple of years to fade.
  • Breasts change over time with ageing, weight fluctuation, hormones and gravity; some people later choose a lift or an implant exchange.
  • Implants are not guaranteed to last a lifetime, so further surgery may eventually be needed.

Risks and safety (ASPS patient information)

ASPS lists the following possible risks of breast augmentation surgery, discussed fully before consent:

  • Anaesthesia risks.
  • Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) or other very rare cancers in the capsule, such as breast implant-associated squamous cell carcinoma (BIA-SCC).
  • Bleeding or haematoma.
  • Changes in nipple or breast sensation.
  • Fluid accumulation (seroma).
  • Tight scar tissue forming around the implant (capsular contracture).
  • Implant leakage or rupture.
  • Infection and persistent pain.
  • Poor scarring, wrinkling of the skin over the implant, or the implant sitting in the wrong position.
  • The possibility that revision surgery will be needed.

For silicone implants, the FDA recommends screening with MRI or ultrasound five to six years after placement and every two to three years thereafter. Risk factors include pregnancy, weight change and the menopause. Routine examinations help confirm that an implant is intact, because a ruptured implant sometimes causes no symptoms.

ASPS patient information

ASPS averages cover the surgeon’s fee only and exclude anaesthesia, operating-room facilities, medical tests, post-surgery garments and prescriptions. Most health insurance plans do not cover cosmetic breast augmentation or a later revision.

Incision sites, scar healing and aftercare

Scars are an expected part of breast augmentation surgery, and where they sit is governed mainly by the incision used to create the implant pocket. Their final appearance depends on incision choice, skin type, genetics, tension on the wound and aftercare. The sections below describe the usual incision options, how scars typically mature and which general measures support healing. Outcomes, risks and suitability vary between individuals, and an in-person medical assessment is required before any treatment decision.

Incision options and where scars sit

Surgeons reach the breast and the implant pocket through a small number of standard routes. The choice balances surgical access, the implant type and implant placement, the surgeon's training, and the patient's anatomy and preferences. Incisions are usually planned so that resulting lines fall within natural skin folds or along the border between skin and areolar pigment, where they are simpler to conceal in ordinary clothing. No incision leaves skin without a mark; planning aims to keep lines discreet rather than absent.

Inframammary fold

The inframammary incision sits in the crease beneath the breast. It provides direct access to the pocket and is used for both silicone and saline devices, as well as for many revision procedures. The line is hidden within the fold when standing, although its visibility changes with posture and clothing. Where the fold is shallow, or where the two sides differ, the surgeon plans the crease position carefully so the scar does not sit too high or too low. Heavier or larger breast implant sizes can place more tension on this line during healing.

Periareolar

A periareolar incision follows the lower border of the areola, where darker and lighter pigment meet. It can be a reasonable option where that border is well defined. The route passes through breast tissue, and surgeons discuss possible implications for nipple sensation and breastfeeding in general terms at consultation. Scar visibility depends on how the line heals along the pigment boundary, and this varies with skin type and individual tendency to pigmentation change.

Transaxillary

A transaxillary incision is placed within the armpit crease, so no scar appears on the breast skin itself. It is used with particular implant types and operative approaches and depends on the surgeon's training and the patient's anatomy. Because the working distance to the breast is longer, later surgery is not always possible through the same route, and some revisions require an additional incision. Consultation therefore covers these limitations alongside the position of the scar.

Comparing the three approaches

ApproachTypical scar positionPoints in favourPoints to discuss
Inframammary foldCrease beneath the breastDirect access; commonly used for primary and revision surgeryLine may be visible in some positions; fold position needs planning
PeriareolarLower border of the areolaPigment boundary can soften the linePasses through breast tissue; healing varies by skin type
TransaxillaryArmpit creaseNo scar on the breast skinTechnique dependent; later access can be limited

How scars mature over time

Scar healing is usually described in overlapping phases rather than fixed stages. In the first weeks the line is commonly pink or red, slightly raised and firm to touch, and itching or tightness is frequent. Over the following months collagen remodels, and the scar typically becomes flatter, softer and paler. Maturation frequently continues for a year or longer, and some lines keep changing beyond that. These descriptions are indicative only; the pace and the final appearance vary widely between individuals.

Skin type and genetics influence the result. Darker skin tones may be more prone to pigmentation change, and some people form raised or keloid scarring whatever the incision used. The skin of the breast also carries tension, particularly with heavier devices, which can widen a line over many months. Terms such as hypertrophic and keloid scarring are explained in the site glossary, which may help when reading clinical letters.

Patients often ask what they will see at each stage. In the early weeks the line may look prominent and feel tight; by the third month it is commonly flatter though still coloured; through the second half of the first year it usually continues to soften. Some people find the scar most noticeable at three to six months and quieter afterwards, while for others change is slow and steady. Clinical photographs taken at follow-up help track progress objectively once memory of the earlier appearance has faded.

General scar care measures

Most surgical teams provide written aftercare instructions, and protocols differ between clinics and between patients. Measures commonly discussed include the following, introduced at the stage of healing your surgeon advises.

  • Protect maturing scars from sunlight. Ultraviolet exposure can darken early scar tissue, so covering the area or using sun protection is commonly advised for several months.
  • Consider silicone gel or sheeting once external healing is complete, following the clinic's instructions on duration and application.
  • Keep incisions clean and dry as directed, and avoid soaking, swimming or heavy sweating until the team confirms it is appropriate.
  • Avoid nicotine completely during healing, because it restricts blood supply to skin and is associated with wound problems.
  • Wear recommended support garments and avoid strain on the incision during the early recovery period.
  • Attend scheduled follow-up so that healing can be assessed and concerns raised early rather than late.

Massage of mature incision lines is advised by some surgical teams and not others, so it should begin only when wounds are confirmed closed and comfortable. Firm pressure over unhealed skin, early underwire bras and adhesive products used too soon can irritate a healing line. If dressings or tapes are used, instructions on when to change or remove them should be followed exactly, and any skin reaction should be reported.

What can make scars less favourable

Several factors can work against neat healing, and many of them are modifiable before and after surgery.

  • Nicotine use of any kind around the time of surgery and throughout healing.
  • Wound tension from heavier implants, early heavy lifting or vigorous upper-body activity.
  • Infection or wound breakdown, which makes widening or distortion of a scar more likely.
  • A personal or family tendency to hypertrophic or keloid scarring.
  • Poor nutrition, poorly controlled chronic conditions, or medicines that affect healing or bleeding.
  • Sun exposure on immature scars, and delayed presentation of wound problems.

These points sit alongside the general breast augmentation risks discussed during consent, and they are reviewed before surgery so that planning reflects individual circumstances.

Scars after fat transfer

Fat transfer breast augmentation avoids implant incisions on the breast in many cases, but small scars remain. Fat is harvested through liposuction access points, commonly on the abdomen, flanks or thighs, and these puncture marks mature like other scars. The marks are usually short, although their number and position depend on the areas treated. Donor areas can also change in contour, and access points may be visible on the skin of the breast where fat is injected. Sun protection, garment use and adherence to aftercare advice apply to donor sites as well as to the breast.

Asymmetry, wide scars and revision scarring

Small differences in scar position, length or width between the two sides are common and often settle as healing progresses. Lines may widen when tension is high, and some patients notice a scar more in certain positions than under clothing. Scar position can also shift slightly as swelling settles and the implant settles into its pocket, so a concern raised at two weeks is assessed differently from one raised at twelve months. Where a scar matures unfavourably, options such as silicone therapy, injections, laser treatment or surgical scar revision can be discussed; these are individualised and are usually considered after maturation is complete. Further breast surgery may reuse an existing line or require a new one, as outlined in breast implant revision. No revision can be promised to produce a particular scar appearance.

When to seek a review

Contact the surgical team promptly if a scar or wound shows spreading redness, increasing warmth or pain, discharge, bleeding, opening of the wound, fever, or a rapidly thickening or painful raised scar. Sudden change in breast shape, a firm painful breast, or a scar that concerns you also warrants review, as does any worry that arises between scheduled visits. Early assessment is preferable to waiting when something feels wrong, and follow-up forms part of the pathway described in breast augmentation surgery patient information.

Scars at your consultation

Useful questions include where scars would sit for your anatomy, which incision suits the planned implant and pocket, how the fold or areolar border is planned, what aftercare is provided, how follow-up is arranged, and how scars are managed if healing is slow. Marketing language implying that surgery can leave skin without marks should be treated with scepticism. This information is educational and is not a substitute for personal medical advice from a qualified clinician.

Scar-care questions

Scars do not disappear entirely. They usually soften, flatten and pale over many months to more than a year, but final appearance varies with skin type, genetics, incision site and healing conditions. Surgeons aim to place incisions where lines can be concealed rather than erased.

Noticeability depends on skin type, healing, clothing and individual preference rather than a single ranking of approaches. Inframammary, periareolar and transaxillary incisions each sit in different anatomical areas with different trade-offs. Suitability is assessed during an in-person consultation.

Early scars are often pink, raised or firm for the first weeks to months, then gradually flatten and fade. Maturation commonly continues for a year or longer, and the timeline varies between individuals. Follow-up review helps track healing.

Nicotine use, wound tension, infection, poor nutrition and delayed healing can all affect scar quality, and sun exposure can darken immature scars. Following post-operative instructions and attending follow-up supports healing. Individual variation remains important.

Questions

Breast augmentation FAQs

Recovery varies according to the procedure, surgical technique, individual healing and the clinician’s advice. Your surgeon will give you a personalised return-to-activity timeline.

No procedure can promise permanent results. Breast implants are not lifetime devices: additional operations may be needed and complications can occur. Fat transfer results depend on how much transferred fat survives.
